item.title: The U.S. already oversees commercial space. Novelty is not a regulatory gap.
item.description: A voluntary federal pilot could determine whether America’s next generation of commercial-space businesses operates under clear, generally applicable rules or must first obtain discretionary government permission merely because an activity is new. The Office of Space Commerce’s new Space Commerce Certification (SCC) pilot program may help coordinate novel proposals, but it could become the basis for, or evolve into, an informal permission system if policymakers misinterpret Article VI of the Outer Space Treaty as requiring a bespoke authorization and supervision regime whenever a commercial mission is unfamiliar. Article VI requires states to authorize and continuously supervise nongovernmental activities in outer space, but leaves each state to determine the domestic form, intensity and timing of those functions; it neither requires mission-specific approval because an activity is novel nor compels a customized federal supervisory regime for each unfamiliar use of a spacecraft.
